articles.title: Mayer vs Cameron: Mikaela Mayer feels 'unbeatable' ahead of title unification fight against Chantelle Cameron
articles.summary: Mikaela Mayer vs Chantelle Cameron will headline MVPW-06 at the bp pulse LIVE arena in Birmingham; WBO, WBA and WBC super welterweight titles on the line in UK vs USA main event; watch MVPW-06: UK vs USA live on Sky Sports on Saturday August 29
articles.body:
British WBO title holder Cameron (22-1, 8 KOs) faces American Mayer (22-2, 5 KOs) at the bp pulse LIVE arena on Saturday - live on Sky Sports - with every bout on the MVPW-06 main card pitting a UK fighter against a US opponent.

WBA and WBC champion Mayer has no shortage of respect for Cameron - who has won her last four fights since a rematch defeat to Katie Taylor in 2023 - but has backed her own ability to unify the titles in front of what is set to be a hostile Birmingham crowd.

"I feel better than ever," Mayer told Sky Sports . "I just know I just feel unbeatable right now. I feel in a great position and I can't wait to get out to the UK and do my thing.

"[Cameron] is good at what she does. She's an aggressive fighter. She lets her hands go.

"She fights at a fast pace and so do I. So that's going to make for a very exciting fight for the fans.

"But I just don't think it's going to be as close and as much of a war as everyone thinks.

"There's probably a handful of people who think I'm stupid for coming to the UK and going onto Chantelle's turf, but I'm just confident in myself right now.

"I'm fighting better than I've ever fought, smarter than I've ever been. And I just believe in myself.

"I feel like no matter where I go, I'm still going to kick butt. So it could be here. It could be there. I'm taking the win."

Mayer pointed to her "versatility" as a defining factor come Saturday, insisting nothing can prepare Cameron for the new and improved version of the 36-year-old that awaits.

"I'm really hard to train for because I've developed so much these last 10 months of being in the gym," Mayer told Sky Sports .

"I know I haven't fought since last October but the things I'm doing now, it's really impossible for Chantelle to have trained for me at this point.

"I'm going to do everything I can to make it a very obvious win, maybe a stoppage, we'll see, but I know I'm coming out with my hand raised.

"I've worked on making sure that my inside game and when I do press forward that my defence is tighter and I'm the one landing my shots. I'll definitely be using a little bit of everything I've got, but knowing mine and Chantelle's styles there will definitely be moments where it will be a dog fight."

'A win would be one of the best moments of my career'

The 35-year-old Cameron won the WBO super welterweight title - a belt Mayer had vacated just months after beating Mary Spencer for it - with a dominant victory over Michaela Kotaskova in April.

The significance of the chance to become unified world champion by reclaiming the WBO crown is not lost on Mayer, with the American describing the prospect of victory as a career-defining moment.

"[A win would be] definitely up there with one of the best [moments].

"I've had a pretty awesome career. Even though I've gone through some ups and downs, I think that's what makes my career even more special and what makes these big fights that are ahead of me extra special.

"I've had to go through trials and tribulations - I've had to adjust, I've had to make changes in my team and keep continuing to get better - and I've done that.

"Going in there and having a dominating performance against someone like Chantelle Cameron, who is very highly respected - the only person to beat Katie Taylor - that's going to definitely be one of the best moments of my career thus far."

The upcoming bout may not be the last between the two, with Mayer revealing that a rematch clause has been included in the contract of both fighters:

"Well, Chantelle and I do have a rematch clause on both of our ends, which is unique, but if it's the type of fight that everyone expects, then why not do a rematch?

"Why not give it to the world again? I have no problem giving a rematch when it's, when it's justified.

"Do I want to kick her butt so bad that she doesn't even want to activate that rematch clause? Of course. But if she does, we can go again."

Watch MVPW-06 in Birmingham, headlined by Mikaela Mayer vs Chantelle Cameron and with Caroline Dubois also in action, live on August 29 on Sky Sports. Get Sky Sports or stream boxing with no contract .

articles.summary: International Sports News: Alex Apodaca just pulled off the kind of result that completely flips a fight card on its head. At DWCS Season 10, Week 3, Apodaca walked into the Met.
articles.body: Alex Apodaca just pulled off the kind of result that completely flips a fight card on its head. At DWCS Season 10, Week 3, Apodaca walked into the Meta APEX as the massive underdog against Bella Mir. UFC's official results had Mir listed as a -6000 favorite, so the expectation was pretty clear before the cage door closed. Three rounds later, Apodaca had all three judges on her side. She won 29-28 across the board and left with something even bigger than the win: a UFC contract.How Alex Apodaca broke down Bella Mir over three roundsThe fight did not turn into an easy night for Apodaca. Mir still managed to land some heavy shots, but Apodaca found ways to make the matchup difficult for her.According to the UFC's official recap, Apodaca kept switching stances and mixed up her striking rather than giving Mir the same look over and over. Her takedown defense was also a major part of the performance. That kept Mir from relying too heavily on her grappling and allowed Apodaca to keep the fight in areas where she was more effective.Nothing was left to a single dramatic moment. The bout went the entire three rounds, with the judges all reaching the same 29-28 score for Apodaca. That consistency made the result even more striking considering the enormous betting gap coming into the contest.Bella Mir leaves with first professional MMA defeatFor Mir, the loss changes an unbeaten record she had carried into the fight. She entered DWCS with a 3-0 professional MMA mark and also had an established name in the sport through her father, former UFC heavyweight champion Frank Mir.After the decision, Mir dropped to 3-1. Apodaca, meanwhile, moved to 8-1 and turned the biggest opportunity of her young career into a place on the UFC roster.Dana White later confirmed contracts for Apodaca along with Nick Galanti, Ronald Humphrey, Sean Clancy Jr., and Guilherme Uriel.Galanti needed only 35 seconds to earn his contract with a knockout. Clancy Jr. finished Gary Balletto in Round 2, while Uriel submitted Mario Piazzon with a standing guillotine.That leaves Apodaca with a very different kind of result. She did not need a finish. She survived three rounds against a heavily favored opponent, got every judge's score, and secured her UFC spot in the process.For now, the biggest number beside her name is simple: 8-1. articles.summary: Bella Mir misses out on a UFC contract after suffering one of the biggest shocks in MMA history by losing to Alex Apodaca.
articles.body:
Bella Mir has missed out on a UFC contract after suffering one of the biggest shocks in MMA history by losing to Alex Apodaca.

Highly-rated prospect Mir, who is the daughter of former UFC heavyweight champion Frank, went into the contest as an overwhelming favourite but was on the losing end of a unanimous decision.

All three judges on Dana White's Contender Series - a show where winners of fights are often rewarded with UFC contracts - scored the contest 29-28 in American Apodaca's favour.

Mir, 23, has said she wants to win a UFC championship, a Brazilian jiu-jitsu title, a Zuffa Boxing belt and an Olympic wrestling gold medal, but the loss puts a dent in the American's ambitions.

After the fight, UFC president Dana White said the pre-fight betting odds, which had Mir as a massive favourite to win, were misplaced.

"You can't have those kind of underdogs on this show. Anything is possible, and if the Bella Mir fight didn't just prove it - the odds were way out of whack," said White.

"This sport's too crazy to be that big of an underdog."

Apodaca, 32, was rewarded with a UFC contract following victory, while Mir suffered the first defeat of her five-fight professional MMA career.

Elsewhere, Scotland's Sean Clancy Jr won a UFC contract after he stopped American Gary Balletto in the second round following a number of unanswered ground strikes.

The 23-year-old, who is the welterweight champion in UK-based promotion Cage Warriors, extended the unbeaten start to his career to nine.

articles.title: Moses Itauma vs Filip Hrgovic: World title would earn British rising star sporting icon status, says Frank Warren
articles.summary: Frank Warren believes Moses Itauma can achieve sporting icon status beyond boxing if he beats Filip Hrgovic to become the second-youngest heavyweight champion in history on Saturday; the 21-year-old Brit fights for the vacant IBF title at London's O2 Arena
articles.body:
Itauma fights Croatian Filip Hrgovic for the vacant IBF heavyweight world title at London's O2 Arena on Saturday.

The undefeated 21-year-old has swept aside all those placed in front of him throughout his 14-fight career and stands on the brink of a historic victory that could shape the heavyweight division for a generation.

Aged 21 years, eight months and one day on fight night, victory would see Itauma become Britain's youngest heavyweight world champion and the second-youngest in history behind Mike Tyson.

"I'll be very proud if that happens," Itauma's promoter Warren told Sky Sports News.

"It will be a fantastic achievement for somebody who's only had 31 professional rounds of boxing and no senior bouts as an amateur.

"He's the best young fighter at this stage of his career that I've been involved with. He's so mature, mentally and physically, as a fighter. He's got a tremendous boxing brain and he's very articulate.

"He's a very smart young man, he's got a very smart brain. He's very level-headed, very humble. But I'll tell you what, he can fight.

"If he comes through, I don't think he'd just be an icon in boxing. He'd be a sporting icon."

Itauma's bout with Hrgovic has had a coming-of-age feel from the moment it was signed in June.

Its elevation to world title status, following unified heavyweight champion Oleksandr Usyk's decision to relinquish the belt, only added further significance.

Hrgovic, whose only career defeat came via a TKO loss to current WBO champion Daniel Dubois, represents a marked step up in opposition.

The 34-year-old is not only bidding to become Croatia's first heavyweight world champion but, like Itauma, has the opportunity to stake a claim in a division in transition.

"Itauma is fighting somebody who's not just coming to show up," Warren added. "He's in with a tough guy, Filip Hrgovic, a really good, tough competitor.

"Hrgovic has only been stopped because of a cut eye. Other than that, he's won all of his fights. He has 15 knockouts in his career and is a former Olympic bronze medallist.

"For him, it's all history-making as well. Where he comes from in Croatia, he'd be the first boxer to win a heavyweight title, so he wants to create history himself.

"All these fighters who are now fighting for the vacant titles are looking to jockey into position because it's an exciting time in the heavyweight division.

"The older generation, like Tyson Fury and Usyk, who didn't want to defend his titles and vacated them, are looking to do other things, so these are the young bucks coming through."

articles.body: Islam Makhachevâs UFC 330 celebrations have sparked another response from Merab Dvalishvili. The former UFC bantamweight champion has posted a video on X to explain why he was upset after seeing a Russian flag inside the Octagon. Dvalishvili made it clear that his comments were not aimed at Makhachev personally.Instead, he said the issue was deeply connected to his Georgian background and his views about the Russian government. His latest message comes after Makhachev accused him of being unhappy with his success and suggested Petr Yan could silence him in their upcoming rematch.Merab Dvalishvili explains why Islam Makhachevâs Russian flag upset himIslam Makhachev made UFC history at UFC 330 after defeating Ian Machado Garry in the main event. The Russian fighter successfully defended his welterweight championship for the first time. During the celebrations, his team brought a Russian flag into the Octagon. That moment caught Merab Dvalishviliâs attention.He previously questioned why Makhachev could celebrate with his national flag when he had not been allowed to bring a Georgian or American flag into the cage during his own UFC title fights. Dvalishvili has now explained his position in detail.Dvalishvili has once again addressed the controversy in a video posted on X. This time, he stressed that he respects Makhachev and his achievements.âI like Islam Makhachev. I think heâs a great and humble champion. I respect all the hard work he has put into his career, I have nothing but respect for him.But when I saw his team bring the Russian flag into the Octagon, I was upset. And the reason I reacted that way is because, first during all five of my UFC title fights, I was never allowed to bring my Georgian or American flag into the cageâ, He wrote.He continued, âSecond reason for me, this is very personal because of what Russian politics and the Russian government have done to my country. From the very beginning he wasnât happy at all about my success in the Octagon, but I donât pay attention to things like that. Heâs already spoken about this many times,â Makhachev said.Makhachev then brought Petr Yan into the discussion. He predicted that Yan would beat Dvalishvili again in their rematch and suggested the result would finally end the Georgianâs criticism.However, Dvalishviliâs latest video attempted to separate his personal respect for Makhachev from his political disagreement. articles.title: His father died young and financial hardship forced him to quit boxing and work as a school security guard; years later, Sumit Kundu survived a career-threatening injury and is now going to the Asian Games
articles.summary: Boxing News: Every era of sport produces a story that transcends the boundaries of an arena. Sumit Kundu's life is a masterclass in raw human resilience, a journey.
articles.body: Every era of sport produces a story that transcends the boundaries of an arena. Sumit Kundu's life is a masterclass in raw human resilience, a journey defined by devastating loss, sacrifices made at a young age, and an incredible comeback against all odds.The early tragedy and big sacrificeBorn in Dhakal village in Jind, Haryana, Sumit took up boxing in 2013, drawn to the discipline and grit of the ring.However, hardship struck early when he lost his father at a young age. To keep the family afloat, his mother began taking on odd tailoring jobs, working endless hours just to provide basic meals.Watching his family struggle under immense financial pressure, Sumit made a heartbreak decision: he hung up his boxing gloves in his teens and stepped away from the sport.Taking a job as a security guard at a local school, the promising athlete put his personal ambitions aside so he could bring home a steady income.A village unites for a second chanceSumit’s story could easily have ended at those school gates. But the elders in Dhakal village knew his raw talent in the ring was too rare to waste.Recognizing his potential, the village community rallied behind him, pooling their personal funds to cover his essential dietary and training expenses so he could quit his job and return to boxing.Repaying their faith with absolute dominance, Sumit surged through the ranks. He secured gold at the National School Games in 2018, dominated the 2019 Khelo India Games, and stunned the national circuit by claiming the Senior National Championship title on his debut in 2021.The prize money from these early victories went straight back into his nutrition and equipment, fueling his rise to international competition.Rising to International StardomBy 2022, Sumit was established as one of Indian boxing’s most exciting prospects.Representing the nation, he clinched a Gold medal at the 2022 Thailand Open and pulled off a stunning upset at the prestigious Strandja Memorial tournament by defeating World Championship silver medalist Dzhambulat Bizhamov.Sumit went on to represent India at the 2022 Commonwealth Games and the World Championships, earning a spot as an Army Havildar through his sports achievements.The career-threatening nightmareJust as his momentum peaked, disaster struck during the national championships during the Paris Olympic qualifiers.Sumit suffered a severe ACL and meniscus tear in his knee, an injury so severe it sidelined him for nearly two years and ruled him out of the Paris Olympics.Following surgery, he spent a grueling year and a half in rehabilitation in Mumbai. Doubts naturally crept in. "Thoughts crossed my mind to quit boxing... After rehab, I didn't feel the same energy in my knees. I felt my boxing career was over," he later admitted.Kept afloat by the guidance of his childhood coach Ved Prakash, his family, and trainers, Sumit pushed through the physical and mental pain to rebuild his lower-body strength from scratch.The unstoppable comebackDropping down to the 70kg weight class, Sumit made his return at the national selection trials for the Commonwealth Games and Asian Games.He delivered a sensational performance, defeating World Cup gold medalist Hitesh Gulia in the semifinals before beating Deepak in the final to seal his official berth.From guarding school doors to standing tall on the international stage, Sumit Kundu has proved that no blow life lands is powerful enough to break a true champion.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Mayer vs Cameron: Alycia Baumgardner scared of GWOAT heiress Caroline Dubois, says Claressa Shields
articles.summary: Claressa Shields has identified Caroline Dubois as the fighter best placed to succeed her as the GWOAT of women's boxing; Shields hails Dubois’ ambition, confidence and hunger ahead of Saturday’s world-title defence against Amelia Moore, live on Sky Sports
articles.body:
WBA, IBF, WBO and The Ring super featherweight champion Baumgardner has consistently dismissed talk of a fight against Dubois, labelling it premature and insisting the British fighter is not yet at her level.

Baumgardner's comments have done little to deter Dubois, who has remained in relentless pursuit of the American since unifying the division above with her victory over Terri Harper in April.

Dubois fights unbeaten former US Olympian Amelia Moore in the co-main event of MVPW-06 in Birmingham, alongside Mikaela Mayer vs Chantelle Cameron, live on Sky Sports this Saturday, and wants Baumgardner next.

As a multi-weight world champion, Shields knows a thing or two about switching weight classes, so she speaks from experience when outlining why she thinks Baumgardner is unwilling to accept Dubois' challenge.

"Honestly, when you've got somebody five pounds bigger than you, beating down your door, barking up your tree, saying what they'll do to you, that they'll beat you up, they'll knock you out, they're calling you out constantly, you would think that Alycia would go up five pounds and just fight and prove her greatness," Shields told Sky Sports.

"I think that Baumgardner is 100 per cent scared of Caroline, and she doesn't want to risk her record now that she already has one loss on it. She doesn't want to risk it. I believe that Caroline will win that fight."

Baumgardner will move up a division to fight Elif Nur Turhan for her IBF lightweight world title on November 8 in a move that could bring a blockbuster showdown with Dubois a step closer.

Since winning back-to-back Olympic gold medals, Shields has conquered every opponent placed in front of her through an unbeaten 19-fight career, becoming a multi-weight world champion and proclaiming herself the Greatest Woman Of All Time.

Only time will tell whether there is a fighter on the planet capable of filling Shields' gloves when she retires from boxing, but she is confident she has already identified the heiress to her throne.

"They asked me who I think is going to carry the torch once I'm gone and I was like, listen, it's going to be Caroline Dubois," Shields added.

"I believe Gabriela Fundora will be a champion to be reckoned with but, right now, Caroline Dubois is right there.

"She's calling out the biggest girls, the best girls, she's trying to make the best fights. She's confident. She's loud. She's mean. She's getting knockouts. She's right on time."

Dubois, the unified WBC and WBO lightweight world champion, is one of the hottest prospects in British and women's boxing and will look to take a step towards undisputed status with victory over Moore in Birmingham.

Shields has taken a keen interest in Dubois' career and has vowed to support her in fulfilling her potential in the sport, whichever direction that may lead.

"Caroline has her own name," Shields said. "If she wants to be called the GWOAT, and she's breaking the records and got the accolades, I'm not going to be mad about it, as long as she's doing GWOAT things, she's fighting the best fighters, and she's winning, and she's racking up the belts.

"I know that my accomplishments are going to be hard to beat. I just became a 21-time world champion last week, but Caroline has the IT factor, and she'll fight anybody.

"I'm going to be there supporting her. If she ever needs me in camp, or anything, she knows that I'll be there. We always joke about sparring; one day it's going to happen.

"She's already asked me [for advice], and I've already given it to her. I just told her to have fun with her career, make her career about her, do whatever she wants to do, and always prepare and never underestimate her opponents."

articles.title: Petr Yan vs Merab Dvalishvili 3, un combate de legado: "Si me gana, será el mejor de la historia"
articles.standfirst: El peleador georgiano tiene claro que el vencedor de este combate se convertirá en el GOAT definitivo de peso gallo
articles.summary: El peleador georgiano tiene claro que el vencedor de este combate se convertirá en el GOAT definitivo de peso gallo
articles.body: El próximo 24 de octubre, Petr Yan y Merab Dvalishvili se medirán en el evento co estelar del UFC 333 para cerrar su trilogía, con el cinturón de peso gallo en juego. Este combate es uno de los más esperados de 2026, ya que es un enfrentamiento que decidirá de manera definitiva quién es el GOAT de la división. Así lo ha hecho saber el peleador georgiano, que sabe que hay en juego mucho más que un título tras perder ante el ruso el pasado diciembre. La primera vez que ambos se vieron las caras fue en marzo de 2023, cuando Yan intentaba ganarse una nueva oportunidad titular tras perder el título ante Aljamain Sterling por descalificación y caer de nuevo en la revancha. Sin embargo, el ganador de ese duelo fue 'The Machine', que dos combates después se convertiría en campeón de la división y asentaría un legado que se extendería durante todo el 2025. Hasta cuatro defensas realizó Merab el año pasado, lo que significó un récord sin precedentes. Umar Nurmagomedov, Sean O'Malley, Cory Sandhagen... Todos cayeron ante el cardio y el grappling de Merab, hasta que la actividad le pasó factura y recibió un correctivo por parte de Yan el pasado diciembre para perder su corona de manera clara por decisión unánime. Por tanto, su tercera pelea será definitoria para definir la rivalidad y quién es el rey absoluto de las 135 libras. "Si él me gana, se convertirá en el mejor luchador de la categoría de peso gallo de la historia. Si yo le gano, seré yo el mejor. Así que no solo está en juego el título de campeón", afirmó Dvalishvili en una entrevista con Red Fury MMA tras hacerse oficial el combate. Si algo tiene la división de peso gallo es que no hay un GOAT definido como pasa en otras divisiones con Jon Jones, Islam Makhachev o Demetrious Johnson. Hace tiempo se consideraba a Dominick Cruz el mejor de la categoría, pero sus lesiones y su dolorosa derrota ante Cody Gardbrandt cambiaron esa visión para muchos. Luego llegó TJ Dillashaw, pero sus escándalos de dopaje le sacaron de la ecuación. De hecho, durante unos meses se llegó a hablar de Aljamain Sterling como el GOAT, aunque más tarde fue Merab el que se ganó ese puesto tras sus cuatro defensas en un año, su carisma, y sus exhibiciones en el octágono que le han convertido en una auténtica superestrella. Sin embargo, Petr Yan ya marcó un antes y un después en su primer reinado al finalizar a José Aldo -GOAT de peso pluma para muchos- y postularse como uno de los mejores strikers de la UFC. A pesar de que fue descalificado en su primera defensa por un rodillazo ilegal, logró ser campeón interino tras dar otra clase a Cory Sandhagen, pero aquella derrota contra Merab y otra polémica decisión contra O'Malley le llenaron de dudas. Sin embargo, ha ganado sus últimos cuatro combates para volver a ser campeón, por lo que en caso de superar a Dvalishvili asentaría un legado a la altura de unos pocos elegidos.

articles.title: Aspirante al título mundial del peso pesado con solo 21 años y 31 asaltos... y nadie duda de que es el favorito
articles.standfirst: Moses Itauma se enfrenta a Filip Hrgovic y si vence se convertirá en el segundo campeón más joven de la historia de la categoría reina tras Mike Tyson
articles.summary: Moses Itauma se enfrenta a Filip Hrgovic y si vence se convertirá en el segundo campeón más joven de la categoría reina tras Mike Tyson
articles.body: El peligro para Moses Itauma (14-0, 12 KOs) es que todo parece preparado para que esta semana dé un golpe sobre la mesa y haga historia. Se enfrenta el sábado al croata Filip Hrgovic (20-1, 15 KOs) por el título mundial del peso pesado de la de la Federación Internacional de Boxeo (IBF) en un combate para nada sencillo, pero para el que parece partir como favorito. Itauma es un púgil en pleno ascenso que aspira a convertirse en el segundo campeón más joven de la historia en la categoría reina tras Mike Tyson. El zurdo británico -aunque nacido en Eslovaquia- ha demostrado hasta ahora ser una máquina de precisión con muchos recursos y un gran poder destructivo. Es el soplo de aire fresco que necesitaba la división, pero debe rematar esta primera fase de su carrera con el título mundial para el salto definitivo al estrellato. Su camino hacia el cinturón mundial se vio allanado en las últimas semanas, pues se incluyó el título absoluto de la IBF que en un principio el británico se tendría que haber disputado en combate contra Frank Sánchez. Quizás la gloria se haya adelantado unos meses, pero en cualquier caso, si echamos cuentas, a Itauma le ha llevado solo 31 asaltos en 14 peleas optar el título de los pesados. Sus grandes triunfos han llegado ante Dillian Whyte y Jermaine Franklin. Es inevitable comparar su trayectoria con la de Mike Tyson, aunque no tienen mucho que ver pues se trataba de épocas muy distintas. ‘Iron Mike’ requirió de 74 asaltos en 27 peleas. De todas estas, sólo James Tillis y Mitch Green llevaron al neoyorkino hasta el final, con mención especial para Jose Ribalta, que fue el más duro de todos aunque cayó en el último asalto. A Itauma le preguntaron durante la rueda de prensa previa al combate si había sido “tratado como un niño prodigio”. El púgil respondió: “He noqueado a todos en el primer o segundo asalto. Jermaine Franklin nunca, jamás, jamás había tocado la lona y venía de una victoria sobre Ivan Dychko. Lo destrocé en cinco asaltos. Cuando dices niño prodigio, hace que parezca un privilegio y yo no diría que he sido privilegiado en el boxeo. ¿Acaso me pusieron a Dillian Whyte en bandeja de plata? No, tuve que hacer todo un campamento de entrenamiento antes de enfrentarme a un luchador”. Itauma puede convertirse en campeón con 21 años, 8 meses y 1 día, y si lo lograra de forma tan precoz será porque es extremadamente bueno y espectacular. Si la oportunidad le ha llegado joven, será porque los Usyk, Joshua, Fury o Wilder están de salida justo cuando emerge un peso pesado muy bien preparado a tan corta edad.

articles.title: Three UFC stars fined for jumping outside the octagon at UFC 329
articles.summary: The Nevada Athletic Commission handed down $2,500 fines on Wednesday
articles.body:
Max Holloway, Paddy Pimblett, and Gable Steveson all faced fines after jumping out of the cage to celebrate at UFC 329 in July.

On Wednesday during the monthly meeting for the Nevada Athletic Commission, the three fighters were each fined $2,500 as punishment for leaping outside the cage after their respective fights were over. The fines were deducted from the fighters' purses, which were withheld by the commission after the event.

There's been an uprising amongst fighters after hearing about the potential penalties being handed down for jumping outside the cage to celebrate a victory.

But commissioners were adamant that the rule isn't changing and fighters have to learn to abide by the law of the land when competing in Nevada. It turns out the rule was specifically made after Khabib Nurmagomedov jumped out of the cage to attack members of Conor McGregor's team after their fight ended at UFC 229 back in 2018.

On that night, Nurmagomedov secured a victory with a fourth-round rear-naked choke submission but he immediately jumped over the cage and engaged in a fight with one of McGregor's teammates.

The melee exploded into the crowd with security and police scrambling to maintain order.

"A pretty rough night for all of us," commissioner Anthony Marnell said during the meeting on Wednesday. "It just can't happen anymore."

Nevada Athletic Commission chairman Dallas Haun doubled down on that statement while explaining that the commission doesn't want to hand down these kinds of penalties but what unfolded between Nurmagomedov and McGregor back in 2018 changed the rules for everybody.

"They're jumping the cage to shake Dana [White]'s hand and we appreciate the difference," Haun explaind. "Someone in the crowd behind Dana screaming something could change that in an instant.

"We're not comfortable, we don't like doing this is these instances, but for the safety of the crowd and having learned from UFC 229 in 2018, we feel very strongly about it."

Ultimately, Holloway, Pimblett and Steveson paid the $2,500 fines, the purses withheld are released and none of them face any other penalties from the incident.

articles.title: Itauma vs Hrgovic: Prince Naseem Hamed says Moses Itauma is a 'million times better' than Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury
articles.summary: British boxing legend Prince Naseem Hamed has described Moses Itauma as "a million times better" than Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury.
articles.body:
Boxing legend Prince Naseem Hamed has described Moses Itauma as "a million times better" than Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury and expects the young British heavyweight to surpass both former world champions.

Itauma, 21, is unbeaten in 14 professional fights and faces Croatia's Filip Hrgovic for the vacant IBF heavyweight title at London's O2 Arena on Saturday.

The Chatham fighter has been touted as the heir to the heavyweight throne, while Joshua and Fury have agreed to meet later this year in their long-awaited all-British showdown.

"Moses is on another level to the likes of Tyson Fury and Tyson would say that himself. Tyson would not want to fight Moses and neither would Joshua," Hamed told BBC Sport.

"If they did I would say they are very brave."

Hrgovic taunts starting to wind me up - Itauma

Itauma v Hrgovic & Mayer v Cameron - all you need to know

Victory would make Itauma the second-youngest heavyweight world champion in history, behind only Mike Tyson.

He will also do it one fight sooner than Joshua did when he won his maiden world title in his 16th pro bout.

Fury has lost twice - both to Oleksandr Usyk - while Joshua has lost four times in 34 pro fights.

"I think Tyson Fury was amazing for British boxing and what he achieved, what he did and brought to the game and how colourful he was as a personality," Hamed, 52, added.

"I think Joshua did an amazing job early in his career to win a world title and be an ambassador for British boxing.

"[But] I can't compare Moses. He is a million times better than them."

'Itauma will defend world titles for as long as he wants'

Hamed was one of British boxing's biggest stars during the 1990s, combining an entertaining fighting style with elaborate ring entrances and a larger-than-life character.

The Sheffield-born fighter became Britain's youngest world champion when he beat Steve Robinson for the WBO featherweight title in Cardiff in 1995, aged 21 and 230 days.

Itauma will miss out on that record by 14 days if he beats Hrgovic.

Hamed, though, says he is not concerned about records and simply wants to see "special fighter" Itauma fulfil his potential.

"Winning a national title as an amateur aged 11 and then having in your head all the way through your amateur career that you'll be world champion at 21 - I visualised that. I think it's very much the same for Moses," he said.

"I'm so confident that Moses is going to be the heavyweight champion of the world. I'm so confident that he'll defend that belt for as long as he wants.

Hrgovic is an underdog despite his superior record against better opposition. The 34-year-old is an Olympic bronze medalist and has only lost once - to current WBO world champion Daniel Dubois in 2024 - in 21 fights.

But Hamed does not expect the fight to prove particularly difficult for Itauma.

"On paper it's a test but I don't think the night that we watch it it will be a test," he said.

"I think it's going to be one of Moses' easiest nights of his career and he'll win a world title."

articles.title: Claressa Shields Eyes Beyonce for Epic Ring Walk Before Boxing Retirement Fight
articles.summary: Claressa Shields has done it all in boxing, but she's hoping to get one more wish before she hangs up her gloves.
articles.body:
Claressa Shields has done it all in boxing, but she's hoping to get one more wish before she hangs up her gloves.

The five-division world champion told TMZ that she would love to have Beyoncé walk her out to the ring before she calls it a career.

"Beyoncé, listen, baby girl. Before I retire," Shields said. "… I need you to walk me out. You pick the song, and only perform 30 seconds, one minute, whatever you decide. Before I retire, I need Beyoncé to walk out the greatest woman of all time, and that's my only request. I won't ask you for nothing else. I won't even ask you for a picture if that's not what you want."

Michael Jordan expected to leave media role

New Grand Theft Auto game leaks confirmed

Shields is coming off a sixth-round TKO victory over Kaye Scott for the unified middleweight titles earlier this month. Before her win, she had rapper Latto accompany her to the ring.

The 31-year-old added that she plans to continue her boxing career until she's 38.

While Shields' next move isn't official, she was recently called out by unified super-welterweight champion Mikaela Mayer, and she appears to be open to a future showdown.

articles.title: Is Moses Itauma really the next Mike Tyson? Why everyone's talking (or not talking) about boxing's Next Big Thing
articles.summary: Itauma, 21, has long been hailed as the next Tyson. On Saturday, the British heavyweight prodigy finally gets his chance. Can boxing's next big thing live up...
articles.body:
Call him Moses. It's easier that way. Easier to say, easier to remember, easier to promote. Call him Moses on the fight poster, the billboard and the on-screen graphics and call him Moses when trying to attract either sponsors or the eyes of the public. Simplify him, in other words. Make him a brand, a product. Think of him as one of those superstars whose power is so great they need only their first name. Think Beyoncé. Think Prince. Think Shaq. Think of all the Brazilian soccer players who achieved international fame with just their first name on the back of their shirt, like Romário, Rivaldo, Ronaldo and Neymar. If it can work for them, it can work for you too, Enriko Moses Itauma.

That is the view of Itauma's team at least. They, with good reason, sensed they had a superstar on their hands the day Itauma hatched and have started to now nudge him toward the light ahead of his IBF heavyweight title fight against Filip Hrgovic on Saturday . To get him the attention his talent deserves, they have made a conscious effort to simplify Itauma for a mainstream audience. That's why his next fight was billed as "Moses X Hrgovic" on the DAZN ad I saw on the big red bus that passed while I began to write this piece. It's also why, on that same bus, we were greeted with the tagline "Britain's youngest ever world heavyweight champion awaits," and why Mike Tyson, the world's youngest, is someone to whom Itauma, just 21 years of age, is often compared.

In fact, ever since he turned professional at 18, Itauma has been compared to Tyson. At first, it was purely an age thing — Itauma, they said, wanted to win a world heavyweight title quicker than Tyson did when bouncing Trevor Berbick, the WBC champion, up and down in 1986 (at the age of 20). Yet the more we got to know Itauma as a pro, the more we noticed other connective tissue as well. Beyond a fondness for the color black, he shared with Tyson an intensity and a ferociousness and a hunger to leave work early. They also both had trouble finding opponents capable of remaining upright in their presence.

Twelve months ago, I wrote something about Itauma's future ; specifically, his search for heavyweight names, led by a belief that he would struggle to find the right ones to aid his development. Since then, he has fought just twice — a first-round stoppage of Dillian Whyte last August, and a fifth-round stoppage of Jermaine Franklin in March — but was so impressive in those two fights that no longer are we seeking on his behalf the right opponents to help him both build and bide his time. Instead, owing to not only his talent but a changing of the guard at heavyweight, Itauma now finds himself already on the brink of becoming the second-youngest heavyweight champion in boxing history. Suddenly, because of the decision of Oleksandr Usyk to vacate his heavyweight titles , Itauma's route to the throne is clearer, his move expedited. Beat Hrgovic on Saturday in London and the IBF heavyweight belt, previously owned by Usyk, will then be Itauma's to take home. Then it's all about defending what he has and solidifying his status as one of the best heavyweights in the world. Then it becomes less about adding well-known names to his record and more about adding other heavyweight titles to his collection.

In light of this, the search now is not so much for opponents but rather attention, recognition, fans. It's all well and good saying that Itauma is the most talked-about young fighter in the world, yet to what extent is that lip service, or hyperbole, and to what extent is it actually true? Moreover, who exactly is talking about Moses Itauma, The Next Big Thing, in 2026? Is it the few people who already know of his immense talent and his rapid rise up the heavyweight division, or is it the many more who, when asked to name a boxer, would struggle to think beyond Muhammad Ali and Mike Tyson?

Because it's something else now, popularity. It can be achieved quickly, yes, but it is also often experienced only in a vacuum, a bubble, an echo chamber. If one happens to frequent that echo chamber on a semi-regular basis, the idea of popularity can in time become distorted, giving a false impression of a person's value. In fact, it is only when one elects to step outside it — to touch grass, as the kids say — that one starts to realize that popularity in one realm does not always equate to popularity elsewhere.

For Itauma, this shift to mainstream prominence will be much harder to achieve than it was for his predecessors. Any comparison with Tyson, for example, seems unfair given the difference in eras. Whereas in the '80s and '90s a fighter like Tyson was everywhere, bigger than the sport and watched by everyone, Itauma, the Tyson of today, is at risk of falling victim to his sport's burning desire to make itself even more niche . Now, in the year of 2026, Itauma doesn't just have to break down opponents, he also has to overcome the existential threat of paywalls, attention spans, restless fingers, and all the alternative options available to the perennially indulged and indecisive. He is indeed a thoroughly modern fighter: one whose name is discussed more on social media than in real-life social situations where eye-contact still counts.

Last year, when asked about his fighter's commercial potential, Itauma's manager, Francis Warren, understandably saw no limit to it. "I know what he's capable of," Warren told me. "He is a [Lionel] Messi, he is a LeBron [James], he is a [Michael] Phelps, he is a Tiger Woods. He is a once-in-a-generation talent who will be a cultural sporting icon, worldwide. There's no doubt in my mind."

Even if he should fall short of that projection — and he likely will — the point still stands: Itauma is considered by most to be a generational talent with the ability to at least dream. Whether widely, or only within the narrowing, sparsely populated corridors of boxing, Moses Itauma is a name being spoken about and a boxer of whom big things are expected. He is the superstar both the heavyweight division and the sport itself crave, particularly at a time when superstars are few and far between. He is also, at age 21, already a pay-per-view headliner.

Which is why, when preparing this piece, I was shocked by the difficulty I had getting people to talk about Itauma, this heavyweight everyone is supposedly talking about. Neither his promoter, nor his manager, nor any member of his coaching team had any inclination to comment on Itauma's ascent, his next fight, those Tyson comparisons, or, ironically, the battle to secure mainstream attention in the age of paywalls.

Perhaps their reluctance to do so suggests a weariness, or is merely a reflection of how often these people are asked about Moses Itauma in 2026. Perhaps they are, to a man, now just tired of talking about him, or have by this stage run out of superlatives to use to describe him. Or perhaps, like the fighter himself, the close-knit team surrounding Itauma can see the upside of maintaining an air of mystery, operating in the shadows and the silence, so to speak. If so, fine, fair enough. As well as it being their right, it is hard not to respect the decision to stay quiet at a time when everybody else is aroused by the sound of their own voice and won't stop selling.

To compensate for the silence from Moses Itauma's inner circle, I tried to think of other voices. The first that came to mind was my father's. He had asked "What's his name?" while driving a car the morning after Itauma had stopped Franklin so impressively in March. When I then repeated Itauma's name to him, my father — an on-off boxing fan more off than on these days — said, "Isn't that the guy who beat Joseph Parker?" To which I said, "No, that was Fabio Wardley." He then, having butchered Itauma's surname a second time, asked me to slowly spell it out for him. So, I did. "I-T-A-U-M-A."

That same day there was another voice of note. This one was heard inside the locker room of a Sunday-league soccer team, often the perfect barometer of how popular someone or something is in the real world. In this room Itauma's name was mentioned only by the center forward, a semi-serious boxing fan, who asked his teammates pre-match, "Did anyone watch that Itauma last night?" Following that … nothing. Just the sound of studs on the ground and Deep Heat sprayed on tight muscles. All except me, the center midfielder, either shrugged or asked, "Who is that?" or "Where is he from?"

When informed that Itauma was British, the right back in particular looked somewhat perplexed. "Doesn't sound British," he mumbled, which resulted in me having to explain to him that Enriko Moses Itauma was in fact born in Kežmarok, Slovakia to a Nigerian father and a Slovakian mother. He then spent four years in Slovakia before moving to Kent, England. That is where he learned to box and where, on the advice of his promoter and his brother, he later changed his name with a view to becoming a famous professional boxer. "Oh," said the right back, clearly no longer interested. "Anyone got any tape?"

Three days later, my father's voice, heard this time inside a coffee shop, said, "I can see what you meant about that Moses …" and abruptly paused, still unsure how to properly pronounce the surname. I then did it for him — " Itauma " — and my father said, "Yeah, that's right. Itauma. A bit good, isn't he? I watched that fight you were talking about. What an uppercut." It was at that point I smiled, pleased to know I had done my part. My part of promotion. My part for the sport. "I knew he must be good," my father added, "because you don't get excited so easily about boxers these days."

He was right. I had not waxed so effusively about a boxer for a number of years, that voice almost lost, and the only thing that reduced the significance of my championing Itauma was the fact that everybody else was — and is now — doing the same; singing the same tune. Some of those serenades belong to experts whose appreciation for Itauma goes back years. Lawrence Okolie, for instance, first met Itauma when the young phenom was just 15 years old and turning up to boxing gyms in his school uniform. He even shared a ring with him at that age.

"He's someone I always thought would be amazing from [a] young [age]," said Okolie, 33, the former WBO cruiserweight champion and now a world-ranked heavyweight in his own right. "When I first saw him, I thought, ' Wow, I haven't had someone give me this type of work in years .' I was thinking, ' If he can do this now, what's he going to be like in the future?' Well, we're starting to find out now, aren't we?"

Asked to then pinpoint what made a teenage Itauma so special, Okolie hesitated, "It's hard to say," not because there was a scarcity of things, but rather because there were so many. By all accounts Itauma was not just excellent at 15, he was also ineffable. "He was very powerful for a young man and very smart in the ring. He was also hard to hit. I remember thinking, ' Oh, this is something different .'

"Also, if I'm not allowed to be myself fully, I know that I'm in there with someone serious. Nine times out of 10 when I'm in the ring — whether I'm fat, slim, cruiserweight or heavyweight — I feel like I can kind of control what is happening in the ring. That's just the feeling I get, even on a s*** day. But with him I was like, 'Rah, if I'm not 100%, this is going to go badly.' That's when I knew — hold on, he's really good. The only other time I have felt that was when I sparred [WBO heavyweight champion] Dan Dubois. With Itauma, I was just thinking, 'OK, this is weird. Why is a 15-year-old making me feel like this ? ' "

Six years later, the privilege of watching Itauma in the gym now belongs to Leigh Wood, the former WBA featherweight champion and training partner of the big man. Each day Wood, a man 17 years Itauma's senior, gets to watch the young heavyweight hit bags and pads and will often train alongside him under the watchful eye of their coach, Ben Davison. He, too, has seen Itauma deal with older, more experienced men with relative ease. He, too, knows the feeling of witnessing something unique and special.

"When he first came down to the gym and I saw him hit the pads, I couldn't believe how fast he was," said Wood. "Then, the first time I saw him spar, he was in with another heavyweight but he was moving like he was a lightweight. He actually moves better than a lot of lightweights.

"It's not just his speed, either. It's his shot selection, the combinations, the setups. We play games in the gym like 'shoulder and knee,' where you have to touch your shoulder and then touch your knee, and I can't believe how good he is at it. That's not because he's big and tall and long. It's because he's two steps ahead of everybody else. He's always thinking about the next move. He's always thinking about setting traps. His ring IQ is unbelievable and he's very composed. It's like he has been there and done it all before. It just comes to him like it's second nature."

Of all the things he did well against Franklin in March, including the execution of that finishing left uppercut, it was perhaps Itauma's composure under pressure that impressed the most. This, after all, was meant to represent his first genuine test as a professional. In Franklin, a man never before stopped, Itauma's team felt as though they had found an opponent who could at the very least ask Itauma a question or two. But instead, as if affronted by the mere suggestion of parity, Itauma proved how different he was from all the rest not with an explanation, or a boast, but by going out there and showing it. "I tried to knock him out in the first and second round to win some people some dough," said Itauma (14-0, 12 KOs) after the fight. "But I thought, 'Maybe not today. ' So I went back to the basics — go down to the body — and then the knockout just came. It's not the shots you load up with. It's the shots you don't see."

Commentating from ringside that night in Manchester was DAZN's Adam Smith, regarded by many as the UK's "voice of boxing." He, like most in the trade, has fallen for Itauma in recent years and considers the southpaw a level above the majority of British heavyweights who came before him. Better yet, Smith was able to find the words and the energy to use his voice to explain to me why.

"What really excites me about Moses," he said, "is the fact that all the other heavyweights of this era, Oleksandr Usyk included, have been raving about him. He sparred with Joe Joyce, Lawrence Okolie and those guys young, and he was later in camp with [Tyson] Fury, and AJ [Anthony Joshua], and they all think he's exceptional. That's the best gauge for me — listening to other fighters. They have shared a ring and time with him and they know what they are looking at.

"He seems to have it all. However, the tests are going to get harder; the chin is going to be tested , and his stamina will be tested. It will happen. Filip Hrgovic is the right move at the right time and he will examine him. Then we'll see where we go from there. But in terms of him being a heavyweight prospect, he's the most exciting one I've seen since Tyson."

Here the familiar voice of Smith carries even greater resonance for the simple fact that he is one of the few remaining members of boxing's fight-night fraternity who has been involved in the sport long enough to have covered Tyson's career from ringside. He is therefore uniquely positioned to compare the two: Tyson and Itauma.

"There was a magnetism about Tyson because he struck fear into his opponents," Smith recalled. "He had an aura of invincibility from early on and then he became the youngest heavyweight champion in history. It looked like no one would touch him.

"It's early stages, but I can understand the [Tyson] comparisons. I get that a lot of it has to do with age, and the fact he [Itauma] could become the second-youngest heavyweight champion in history, but I know why those promoting him would make that comparison.

"Tyson was a one-off in many ways, which makes it really difficult to compare Moses, or any fighter, to Mike Tyson. But of all the heavyweights I've seen in the last 40 years of following the sport, I don't think I've been this excited about a heavyweight.

"From my point of view, having watched [Evander] Holyfield and [Lennox] Lewis and the next brigade come through — the Klitschkos [Vitali and Wladimir] and the likes of Joshua — I think there are a number of good heavyweights who have come since Tyson, but in terms of aura, this one feels different. It's not an aura of intimidation, but there's an expectation that he's going to be predatory in the ring, and he's got the hand speed and the boxing IQ to deal with these early opponents with ease."

As for Leigh Wood, he isn't certain whether his training partner will ever one day be as big as Tyson — will anyone? — but he knows this much: Moses Itauma will leave his own mark on the sport.

"I think it's an age thing, yeah," Wood said in answer to the Tyson comparison, "but he's also a bit of a maverick like Tyson. He's a special talent coming through. He's going to be on that pound-for-pound list very soon, and one day, in my opinion, he's going to be the best fighter these shores have ever produced. All the other stuff," meaning popularity, "isn't important at this stage. I feel like nowadays it's mostly about social media, but I just think his performances will be enough to get him the attention. People won't be able to ignore him. He'll make his own noise. He'll keep picking up titles, he'll keep winning in great fashion, and the results will speak for themselves."

By virtue of his connection with DAZN, Smith has a firmer grasp of — and interest in — Itauma's growing stature and popularity. He realizes both how important it is to not hide Itauma from the casual sports fan and how different the landscape is today compared to previous eras in which he has commentated.

"It's funny, my brother was asking me about [Itauma] yesterday," said Smith. "He's a casual fan and he said to me, 'I'm sort of sick of the whole AJ and Fury thing.' He said he doesn't like the 'arrogance' they show after a win. 'But there's something different about Moses,' he said. 'He seems like a normal guy.'

"AJ had the Sky [Sports] platform behind him, which catapulted him, and you've got to give him and his team phenomenal credit for the star they built and all those stadium shows. Tyson [Fury], in a different way, became a star because of his incredible personality and the fact he is a brilliant fighter. In their era there was something really exciting about boxing and it was coming into a whole new realm. Then social media got hold of it and now you've really got to fight to become that star, because there are so many different avenues and streaming platforms. It's great being at DAZN now because we've got the lion's share of boxing and it's fantastic, but it's true that Frank [Warren, Itauma's promoter] has a slightly harder job, because there's no Olympic gold medal [for Itauma], there's not the broad platform that Sky could offer [in years gone by], and people just have more choice now.

"But I think the heavyweights are different," Smith added. "Yes, for a lighter-weight fighter, it might be incredibly difficult to get noticed nowadays. But there is something about the heavyweight division that casual fans absolutely love. All it took were a few of Moses' knockouts and highlight reels to go viral and his social media following shot through the roof. That can happen if you're a heavyweight. We've seen the talent and the excitement, those of us in the trade, but I don't think it will be long before he starts to pierce through into the wider sporting public."

Five months after the last time, I was back in the same changing room on a Sunday morning for the first game of a new season and heard that name again: Moses Itauma .

This time it was evident that a couple more of my unwitting, makeshift focus group were now hip to him, and one or two were even intending to watch him box the following weekend in an IBF heavyweight title fight against Filip Hrgovic. This time there was a bit more knowledge and conviction in the chorus of voices around me. One of them, the goalkeeper, said, "I think he'd beat Joshua and Fury now," to which another, the left back, said, "Yeah, definitely. They're past it, those two. He's the future, I think."

The left back then mentioned that Itauma's upcoming fight had a world heavyweight title on the line, which immediately spread confusion among the few who cared and knew how to watch it . "Isn't that Usyk the heavyweight champion, though?" asked the right winger, lacing his boot. "He beat Fury, didn't he?" The left back: "Yeah, but I swear they said on talkSPORT that Itauma is fighting for the world title. They said that if he wins he will become the youngest world heavyweight champion since Tyson or something."

Content just to listen, the center midfielder on this occasion said nothing. On another day, had I been more enthused to further promote Itauma, I might have provided answers or said to them all, "Just watch him. You'll see. You'll see what everybody is struggling to put into words." But sometimes even the most useful gesture will feel like a thankless task when advocating for a lawless sport prone to bouts of self-sabotage. Sometimes you only wish life was simple; as simple as Moses Itauma makes hard fights.

Elliot Worsell is a boxing writer whose byline first appeared in Boxing News magazine at the age of 17. He has, in the 20 years since, written for various publications, worked as press officer for two world heavyweight champions, and won four first-place BWAA (Boxing Writers Association of America) awards. In addition to his boxing writing, Worsell has written about mixed martial arts for Fighters Only magazine and UFC.com. He has also written two non-fiction books, one of which, Dog Rounds, was shortlisted at the British Sports Book Awards in 2018. He lives in London, England and his writing can currently be found at Uncrowned.com and Boxingscene.com.

articles.title: Mayer vs Cameron winner cements status in top five women's boxers of all time, says Nakisa Bidarian
articles.summary: Nakisa Bidarian believes the winner of Mikaela Mayer vs Chantelle Cameron will cement their place among the top five female fighters in boxing history but tips Caroline Dubois to lead women’s boxing into a new era; watch MVPW-06 live on Sky Sports
articles.body:
The WBO, WBA and WBC titles are on the line when Mayer and Cameron headline MVPW-06 at Birmingham's BP Pulse LIVE Arena this Saturday, live on Sky Sports .

Bidarian, CEO of Most Valuable Promotions, believes Cameron is already in the conversation to be one of the greatest women's boxers by virtue of beating Katie Taylor in their epic two-fight rivalry in 2023.

"The winner cements themselves as one of the top five fighters in history," Bidarian told Sky Sports.

"Chantelle Cameron has to be considered one of the GOATs because she beat Katie Taylor, and she almost beat Katie Taylor a second time, and Katie Taylor undoubtedly is one of the GOATs of women's boxing.

"If Mikaela Mayer can go in there and beat Chantelle Cameron decisively, she'll be one of the GOATs.

"But Cameron is already one of the greatest of all time and whatever time she has left in her career, she's going to be one of the faces of the sport alongside Mikaela as well."

With Taylor one farewell fight away from bringing the curtain down on her illustrious boxing career, and rival Amanda Serrano chasing the women's knockout record and a 50th career victory before hanging up her gloves, a vacancy as the face of women's boxing could soon emerge.

But, aged 36 and 35 respectively, Bidarian believes the baton will be passed to someone else featuring on Saturday's fight card.

"When I think about the future, when Amanda and Katie transition into the next phase of their personal lives and professional careers," Bidarian added.

"We have other fighters on this card that are going to represent that movement, starting with Caroline Dubois."

Britain's Dubois looks to retain her WBC and WBO lightweight titles against unbeaten former US Olympian Amelia Moore in the co-main event of MVPW-06 in Birmingham.

Alycia Baumgardner, a long-time rival and potential future opponent of Dubois, is set to be in attendance at ringside, but Bidarian has urged the 25-year-old to focus on matters inside the ring.

"It's going to be a very exciting fight week and fight night," Bidarian said.

"Alycia Baumgardner will be there, but Caroline has a very formidable opponent ahead of her. You cannot discount Amelia Moore just because she's 4-0.

"She has a rich amateur pedigree. She's also competed in Team Combat League, which is a different boxing product in the US, and she's a strong athlete.

"I'm focused on what happens on fight night. I think it's an absolute challenge for Caroline. It'll be interesting to see what version of Caroline Dubois we get."

articles.title: Umar Nurmagomedov, en busca de la grandeza: "Quiero ganar el cinturón de la UFC"
articles.standfirst: El primo de Khabib tiene como objetivo vencer a Song Yadong este sábado en el UFC Shanghái para volver a obtener una oportunidad titular
articles.summary: El primo de Khabib tiene como objetivo vencer a Song Yadong este sábado en el UFC Shanghái para volver a obtener una oportunidad titular
articles.body: Este sábado, Umar Nurmagomedov (20-1) se medirá a Song Yadong (23-9-1, 1NC) en el UFC Shanghái con el objetivo de dar un golpe sobre la mesa en territorio enemigo y así volver a acercarse al título para cumplir con las expectativas que ya han cumplido el resto de la familia Nurmagomedov. Así lo ha hecho saber recientemente, además de su intención de medirse a Merab Dvalishvili para vengar su única derrota profesional. El 'Team Khabib' es una fábrica de campeones históricos. 'The Eagle' (29-0) se retiró invicto tras arrasar en el peso ligero de la UFC y conseguir el cinturón, Islam Makhachev (29-1) le tomó el testigo y dobló la apuesta consiguiendo el doble cinturón en peso ligero y wélter, y su hermano Usman Nurmagomedov (22-0) lleva mucho tiempo siendo el rey indiscutido en 155 libras en PFL. Umar iba camino de hacer lo propio cuando la UFC le dio la oportunidad titular ante Merab Dvalishvili en enero de 2025, pero falló en el intento. Sin embargo, se ha repuesto de la mejor manera posible venciendo a dos duros oponentes como Mario Bautista y Deiveson Figueiredo, por lo que otra victoria ante Yadong le dejaría a las puertas de volver a pelear por un cinturón que le quitaría un gran peso de encima. "Quiero ganar el cinturón de la UFC. No porque quiera demostrar que soy esto o aquello, sino porque quiero convertirme en campeón solo por mí mismo, por mi padre que tanto ha invertido en mí, por mis hermanos que creen en mí y por Khabib en particular. Quiero repetir su historia para que nuestro legado sea aún mayor", sentenció en una entrevista con 'Red Corner MMA' Más allá del título de peso gallo, que estará en juego el próximo UFC 333 -24 de octubre- entre Petr Yan y Merab Dvalishvili, Umar ha dejado claro que quiere resolver sus cuentas pendientes con el peleador georgiano aunque no tenga el cinturón en sus manos. 'The Machine' no solo le quitó el invicto al primo pequeño de Khabib, sino que le remontó tras perder los dos primeros asaltos e incluso se burló de él. De hecho, han tenido varias acaloradas discusiones que demuestran que no se llevan bien y su rivalidad no es meramente deportiva, e incluso Merab dio una bofetada a un amigo de Umar durante un evento de lucha en Georgia. "Creo que me enfrentaré a Merab, gane o pierda. Ahora es algo personal, no solo para mí, sino para todo Daguestán", reveló en otra entrevista con Mike Bohn. Para que ese suceda, primero Umar tendrá que superar a un duro oponente como Yadong, que contará con el apoyo de la grada y que sabe que una victoria ante el daguestaní sería un paso de gigante en su carrera y un golpe sobre la mesa para demostrar que ha madurado y está preparado para obtener el oro en una categoría llena de talento en la parte alta.

articles.title: Mayer vs Cameron: Amelia Moore ready to scupper Caroline Dubois vs Alycia Baumgardner plans on biggest night of fascinating career
articles.summary: Amelia Moore warns not to look 'beyond her' as opponent Caroline Dubois is linked to world title mega-fight against Alycia Baumgardner; watch MVPW-06 live on Sky Sports, headlined by Mikaela Mayer against Chantelle Cameron in Birmingham
articles.body:
Sure, it is all very Christopher Nolan, all very caped crusader, all very masked man, but the American shoulders her own hardship as immunity to retreat across life both in and out of the ring.

The 36-year-old carries a young professional record of 4-0 as she, in the words of champion Dubois this week, comes 'back onto the radar' to challenge for the Londoner's WBC and WBO lightweight world titles.

From childhood emancipation to Olympic heartbreak, she is well versed in resilience. She will keep coming, like she always has done. Ask Moore and she might tell you she has always been on the radar.

"I had a fight a couple of years ago, I got headbutted and it broke my nose," Moore tells Sky Sports. "I took a punch and shattered my nose, I was bleeding everywhere and it just did not matter.

"There's something inside of me that, in a lot of the time those dark places that people get, I feel like I've been here before.

"It's like in Batman with Bane, he goes, 'I was raised in the darkness'. And I think that's when you are truly comfortable being in uncomfortable places, it's normal to you.

"No matter what, you dig deep, you believe in yourself and you push through."

Moore grew up on a farm in Maine before being emancipated at the age of 16, later working two jobs to fund her life throughout high school, which is where she would also first begin boxing.

Financial circumstances saw her turn towards military opportunities as opposed to the conventional college route, with Moore eventually joining the U.S. Naval Academy. Having been recruited to run track, she also trained in boxing, wrestling and swimming until being medically discharged following her diagnosis of Crohn's disease.

"I didn't know what an allowance was, there was responsibilities that required your attention, and that sacrifice and selflessness was kind of built into me at a really young age," she explains of her childhood.

"My life has been obstacle and challenge, perseverance, and I've created it. I've created that, who I am and who I've become has had to be my effort. There's been no artificial push. There's been no handouts.

"There are times where things get so tough and you think to yourself, why me? You get older and you look back and you're like, thank God it was me. You become resilient, you become creative, you become all of these facets that without a stressor you would never be able to adapt and change and grow."

Moore was previously part of Team USA for three Olympic cycles having reached the 2016 Summer Games qualifying tournament after just 14 official fights.

She was subsequently forced to withdraw through illness, before also missing out on travelling to Tokyo as an alternate in 2020 as a result of COVID restrictions.

On the surface her professional record may speak to that of an unproven, unknown underdog in the face of a greatness-chasing Dubois, but Moore deems her vast amateur pedigree and accompanying tribulations as evidence of her worth on this weekend's platform.

With it comes a chance to tear up the narrative.

"There's a line that I love in a song, it says it's not about a matter of luck, it's just about a matter of time. The timeline isn't what we think it is," she adds. "2020 really broke my heart because I knew that I felt ready, but there was something else meant for me. So you just have to sit with it keep building."

"If you keep persevering eventually you get to this point where it's about being undeniable, and eventually the door opens and opportunity comes, but you have to be ready. I'm ready, I'm ready for this moment.

"We'd all love to be spoon fed and live in a padded world, but those people that don't experience life don't change the world. You can't be bitter, you just have to be better."

While Moore has been gearing up for the biggest test of her career to date, she has also watched on as opponent Dubois continues to be linked to a clash with WBA, IBF, WBO and The Ring super featherweight champion Alycia Baumgardner.

"Everything that's been going on in the background, and then the announcement of the fight between Baumgardner and Elif Nur Turhan , there's already been news articles talking about Caroline's next fight," said Moore.

"Everyone's talking about beyond me. Let them. Go ahead. Come Saturday night, it's just she and I. So that's totally fine.

"Go ahead and keep thinking beyond me, but I know where I am, and I'm still focused on what I need to do."

Moore has trained in martial arts since childhood, she is a former Elite National Championships and National PAL gold medallist, a seasoned Team USA athlete, she is a ringside analyst, she is writing a book, she is an advanced Emergency Medical Technician and she bakes a mean sourdough bread.

A multi-faceted, multi-talented life and career also sees her rub shoulders with boxing's best, Moore having notably worked with undefeated great Terence Crawford in Colorado Springs.

"His entire team has been a great integral part into not only just like my development, but the amount of things that I've learned from Bud," she says.

"I remember the first time I trained with him, I always felt like I was the crazy one. I trained really hard, I don't know if I've ever met anybody that trains harder than I do, or is as dedicated and as crazy disciplined, and then I met him and was like oh my gosh, he's a lot like me.

"I was blown away. All of his team, all of his coaches, they're amazing."

articles.title: Itauma vs Hrgovic: Croat says he will send British heavyweight "back to high school"
articles.summary: Filip Hrgovic tells British heavyweight Moses Itauma he will "send him back to high school" when they fight for the vacant IBF heavyweight world title on Saturday.
articles.body:
Filip Hrgovic told British heavyweight Moses Itauma he will "send him back to high school" when they fight for the vacant IBF heavyweight world title at London's O2 Arena on Saturday.

Unbeaten Itauma, 21, is aiming to become the second-youngest heavyweight world champion in history - Mike Tyson remains the youngest.

Hrgovic, 34, has repeatedly called Itauma a "kid" in the build-up, prompting the Chatham heavyweight to admit the taunts were starting to wind him up.

But Itauma played down their impact at Thursday's news conference. "At the end of the day, talk is cheap. It's schoolboy banter," he said.

An Olympic bronze medallist with an extensive amateur pedigree, Hrgovic's only pro defeat came against Daniel Dubois in 2024.

He dismissed suggestions he was trying to play "mind games".

"I just tell you what I think. I think he's a kid, he's not mature enough. I think I'm the man. I'm a much better age, much more experienced. That's it," he said.

Itauma 'million times better' than Fury and Joshua - Hamed

Hrgovic taunts starting to wind me up - Itauma

Itauma v Hrgovic & Mayer v Cameron - all you need to know

Itauma kept a straight face as Hrgovic continued: "I will smash the kid on Saturday and I'll send him back to high school."

Itauma has stopped 12 of his 14 opponents and has built a reputation for his devastating speed, power and timing.

"The perfect performance will be to go a couple of rounds and close the job," he said. "Same script, different story."

"We'll see, man. No-one ever knocked me out any time in my life," he said. "I only got stopped by Dubois because of cuts and I was in terrible shape because of sickness."

The pair shared an intense face-off before Itauma left the stage.

Hrgovic then made light of Itauma's earlier claim that the Croat had been shaking during a previous face-off, by telling reporters: "Look how much I'm sweating. Look how scared I am."

Itauma refuses to bite back to Hrgovic jibes

Thursday's news conference was held at Studio 338 on London's Greenwich Peninsula, a venue more accustomed to booming club nights and electronic music than heavyweight boxing.

A relaxed, shirtless Hrgovic arrived half an hour before the event and waited patiently as a member of his team fanned him down.

Itauma arrived minutes before the start.

Hrgovic, now wearing a shirt with the buttons undone, described Saturday's fight as "the biggest fight of my life". He questioned whether Itauma was in the right shape and continued to try to provoke a reaction.

Itauma looked slightly agitated but, as he has throughout his career and the build-up to this fight, was reluctant to bite back.

"Me standing in front of a camera and microphone, saying what I'm going to do, doesn't mean much. I'm not trying to engage in any back and forth. My eyes are solely on Saturday," he said.

At 21 years and 244 days, Itauma would become the second-youngest heavyweight champion in boxing history, behind only Tyson, who won the WBC title at 20 years and 145 days in 1986.

Itauma would also become the second-youngest British world champion in any weight division, just 14 days older than 'Prince' Naseem Hamed, who was 21 years and 230 days old when he won the WBO featherweight title in 1995.

But Itauma said he was not interested in records.

"I'm not trying to become the second-youngest heavyweight champion of the world. I'm trying to beat Filip Hrgovic and become world heavyweight champion," he insisted.

The final word - keeping in tone with the event - went to Hrgovic, who ended the news conference by repeating his prediction: "I'll smash the kid, man."

articles.title: Mayer vs Cameron: Alycia Baumgardner turns reporter as Mikaela Mayer and Chantelle Cameron eye fight of the year
articles.summary: Chantelle Cameron said she is in the form of her life and called on Mikaela Mayer to deliver the fight of the year when the two headline in Birmingham on Saturday night; Alycia Baumgardner also appeared at Thursday's press conference; watch MVPW-06 live on Sky Sports
articles.body:
Not a reporter named Alycia, but instead a familiar foe in former undisputed world champion Alycia Baumgardner, who had claimed a front row seat at Thursday's press conference in Birmingham ahead of Mayer's blockbuster world title fight against Chantelle Cameron.

Baumgardner herself had been speaking just minutes earlier following the announcement of her November 8 clash with Elif Nur Turhan. The question? Mayer's mindset, growth, and why Saturday night's fight is different. Different, presumably, to their own fight.

"I've got better and better and better, I've learned not to make the mistakes I made with you," said Mayer.

"When I get in there I'll start quick, start fast, not letting anything get away from me, not leaving it to the judges, because you can't always trust the judges."

Mayer, who navigated an unwelcome reunion impressively, suffered a split decision defeat to Baumgardner in the pair's world title unification bout at The O2 in October 2022, a fight she previously said she believes she won.

But this was not about a rivalry between Mayer and Baumgardner, the latter of whom is instead seemingly on a path towards a potential showdown with Caroline Dubois, should both win their upcoming fights.

On Saturday it is Mayer and Cameron who take centre stage in a collision of two premier technicians amid their respective pursuit of greatness.

"I'm in the stage in my career, these are the only type of fights I really want," said Mayer. "We've had similar careers, a lot of ups and a few downs, but we both always wanted to fight our best.

"We are at the top of our game and navigated our way back to the top."

There are currently few, if any, better fights to be made in women's boxing, with predictions enduring a fence-sitting theme and the winner tipped or a seat among the best to ever lace up the gloves.

"Let's go get fight of the year," said Cameron.

Cameron is famously the only fighter to hold a win over Katie Taylor in the great Irishwoman's professional boxing career, as much feeding into a narrative seeking to nudge Saturday's victory towards iconicity.

She arrives as owner of the WBO super welterweight title, while Mayer occupies the WBA and WBC belts.

Both have hurdled setbacks to return to the top of the sport, Cameron having been denied in her rematch against Taylor and Mayer on the wrong side of what she deemed to be unjust decisions against both Baumgardner and Natasha Jonas.

"I've had a few ups and downs but I'm in a good place. I think I'm in the form of my life," said Cameron.

"I think Mikaela is very good, she's brilliant, I'm a fan of hers. I watch her and enjoy it, it's why I wanted to fight her, I want to fight the best.

"Styles make fights, Mikaela's style is different to Katie Taylor, I think our styles gel for a really good fight."

Mayer this week insisted it was 'impossible' for Cameron to train for her such was her new boxing arsenal, believing that her versatility will prove the difference come Saturday's main event.

"I think I can just do more. You look at her style, it's very straightforward, I'm a little more diverse," said Mayer.

"When I need to switch up the game plan if need be, I can, I have other tools in my pocket. Sometimes in these big fights you have to adjust, and if I have to I have what it takes."

Saturday's chief support will see Dubois defend her WBC and WBO lightweight world titles against America's Amelia Moore.

The Londoner admitted she affords herself the chance to envision the future such are her lofty ambitions in the sport, which may well feature Baumgardner. But despite being heavily linked to a mega-fight against the American, insisted there should never be doubts over her preparations for an opponent, including Moore.

"I'm 100 per cent confident, I've come so far, I've changed my team, moved to LA, dedicated myself and I'm excited," said Dubois. "It's an opportunity to show the world why I'm the best in the 135lb division.

"I always have an issue with people saying about overlooking opponents, I'm a person who believes in goals, big goals, little goals. Little goals can be training, big ones can be becoming undisputed, my mind and heart and soul is set on being undisputed, nobody will stop me achieving that.

"I see respect as training as hard as I absolutely can, I've trained like an absolute animal and left no stone unturned. There's no way I've looked past her."
